name: Autosomal Recessive Spastic Ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay
aliases: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (SACS)

clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia caused by biallelic SACS mutations affecting sacsin, first described in the Charlevoix-Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region of Quebec but now recognised worldwide.
Characterised by the combination of cerebellar ataxia, pyramidal spasticity and peripheral neuropathy.
Classic onset is in early childhood as gait difficulty emerges when learning to walk, although later-onset variants are increasingly reported.
Fundoscopy may reveal thickened, hypermyelinated retinal nerve fibres radiating from the optic disc, a distinctive though not universal sign.
MRI often shows superior cerebellar vermian atrophy with linear pontine hypointensities (pontine stripes), a bulky pons and a hyperintense rim around the thalami.
The peripheral neuropathy shows mixed demyelinating and axonal features, with pes cavus and distal amyotrophy developing over time.
Spasticity may dominate early while cerebellar signs and neuropathy progress, and lower-limb spasticity can later be masked by neuropathic weakness.
Sacsin is a very large chaperone-related protein important for mitochondrial network dynamics and neurofilament organisation.
reference.pathophysiology: ARSACS is caused by loss-of-function variants in SACS, one of the largest human genes, encoding sacsin. Sacsin is a modular protein combining chaperone-like domains, including a J-domain that recruits Hsp70 chaperones, and it contributes to protein quality control, regulation of mitochondrial network dynamics and organisation of the intermediate neurofilament cytoskeleton. When sacsin is deficient, mitochondria become abnormally distributed and neurofilaments accumulate within neurons, disrupting the function of cells with large, highly branched architectures. Cerebellar Purkinje cells degenerate to produce ataxia, corticospinal tract involvement produces the pyramidal spasticity, and peripheral nerves are affected to give a mixed neuropathy. The distinctive hypermyelination of retinal nerve fibres and the characteristic pontine and cerebellar imaging changes reflect this combination of central and peripheral neuronal and myelin pathology.
additionalDifferentials: Complicated hereditary spastic paraplegias with cerebellar features
Other autosomal recessive cerebellar and spastic ataxias including SPG7 and the oculomotor apraxia ataxias
Cerebral palsy, a common misattribution in early childhood cases
Multiple sclerosis and other acquired demyelinating disease
Metabolic leukodystrophies presenting with spastic ataxia
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI for superior vermian atrophy, linear pontine hypointensities, thalamic rim change and a bulky pons
Fundoscopy and optical coherence tomography for a thickened retinal nerve fibre layer
Nerve conduction studies demonstrating a mixed demyelinating and axonal neuropathy
SACS sequencing accounting for the large gene, or a recessive ataxia panel
Retinal imaging to document the hypermyelinated fibres
Screening for treatable mimics including vitamin E deficiency and metabolic causes
redFlags: Rapidly worsening spasticity with loss of ambulation
Development of bulbar or swallowing difficulty
Marked cognitive decline, which is atypical and should prompt reassessment
reference.prognosis: ARSACS is progressive, with spasticity and ataxia worsening over years and loss of independent walking commonly occurring by the fourth or fifth decade. Lifespan may be reduced in advanced disease through immobility-related complications.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing early-onset cases as cerebral palsy because gait difficulty begins in infancy.
Overlooking the characteristic MRI pattern of pontine stripes and superior vermian atrophy.
Failing to examine the fundus for the hypermyelinated retinal nerve fibres.
Assuming the disorder is confined to Quebec, when SACS mutations occur globally.
references: Hereditary ataxia and spastic ataxia reference reviews
management: Care is supportive and multidisciplinary because no treatment halts the disease; physiotherapy and occupational therapy maintain mobility and function
Manage spasticity with agents such as baclofen or tizanidine and focal botulinum toxin, alongside a stretching regimen
Provide ankle-foot orthoses, mobility aids and foot care for the mixed demyelinating-axonal neuropathy, pes cavus and distal amyotrophy
Support balance and gait rehabilitation, falls prevention, and speech and swallowing therapy as the disease progresses
Undertake surveillance for scoliosis and foot deformity, and ophthalmic review of the hypermyelinated retinal fibres
Offer genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance
Coordinate long-term care through a neurology-led multidisciplinary team
